Background

Where do bees go in the winter? And how do they survive?

New common eastern bumblee (Bombus impatiens) queens (gynes) nest underground after mating in the fall. They start new colonies the following spring. Given that, how do they survive rain and snow during their hibernation, which may last for months?

A lab accident led to the discovery that bees may be able to survive submersion (“Hibernating Bumblebee Queens Can Survive Underwater for up to a Week, Study Finds,” n.d.).

1

During an experiment focused on the impact of insecticides on common eastern bumblebees, a graduate student was keeping bee queens in soil-filled tubes in the refrigerator (to mimic winter conditions). One day she noticed some of the tubes were filled with water. She quickly removed the bees but expected them to be dead. Instead, 20 out of 21 were still moving.

This may be an example of where statistics is not needed. Why?

2

A follow-up study submersion (Rondeau and Raine 2024) experiment compared survival under three different conditions.

  • control (no water)

  • floating in water

  • maintained underwater via a plunger

Bees were initially placed in soil filled tubes and refrigerated. After 7 days, submersion treatments were applied. For the treatments with water, bees were maintained for 8 hours, 24 hours, or 7 days. A total of 143 bees (17 control, 21 in each duration x treatment condition) were used. After the experiment, all bees were returned to new tubes with soil, returned to the refrigerator, then assessed for survival at one, four, and eight weeks following the beginning of submersion treatments.

For our exam, we will focus on the data collected at eight weeks following 24 hour submersion treatments. Below code creates a table if you wish to use the combined data. Note the following columns are used

  • Submersion

    • treatment (control; floating, underwater =submerged)

  • Weight

    • weight in mg (measured before the study)

  • Survival

    • 1= survived; 0 = did not survive
bee_data <- read.csv("data_flooding.csv", stringsAsFactors = T)
library(plyr)
bee_data$Submersion <-revalue(bee_data$Submersion, c("ctl"="control")) 
bee_data <- bee_data[bee_data$Time==8 & bee_data$Duration==24 & bee_data$Weight != "NA"|
                       bee_data$Time==8 & bee_data$Submersion=="control" & bee_data$Weight != "NA",]
bee_table <- table(bee_data[bee_data$Time==8 & bee_data$Duration==24|
                       bee_data$Time==8 & bee_data$Submersion=="control","Submersion"],
      bee_data[bee_data$Time==8 & bee_data$Duration==24|
                       bee_data$Time==8 & bee_data$Submersion=="control","Survival"])
colnames(bee_table) <- c("Survived", "Did not survive")
bee_table
            
             Survived Did not survive
  control           2              12
  floating          2              17
  underwater        1              15

5

Data was also collected on the weights of the bees (Weight column in bee_data). Plot the weight data to consider differences among submersion treatments.

library(Rmisc)
library(ggplot2)
bee_summary <- summarySE(bee_data, measurevar="Weight", groupvars="Submersion")
ggplot(bee_summary, aes(x=Submersion, y=Weight)) +
    geom_point(size=3) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=Weight - ci, ymax=Weight + ci), width=0) +
    ylab("Mass (mg)") +
    xlab("Treatment") +
    ggtitle("Mass by submersion treatment")
